Module Five Activity¶

For the module five activity, you will write Python code to create clear and informative data visualizations from the provided data set Most-Recent-Cohorts-Field-of-Study.csv. Your code should be well-organized and reflect a clear understanding of each step in the visualization process.

Note: there are two parts to this assignment. Part One is the data visualization coding activity. Part Two is the reflection paper.

Once your code is complete, you will download this notebook as an HTML file by clicking File, then Download As, then HTML (.html) from the Jupyter menu bar. Validate that your code, output, and all six visualizations (rendered as images using the display() function) are visible in the html file before submission.

Missing Blocks: Ensure that you have clicked Run for all blocks before downloading as an HTML file or the block may be missing from your submission. Images must be called using the display() function, for example: display(Image(filename="output/{image_name}.png"))

Specifically, you must address the items from the rubric criteria.

Part One: Data Visualization¶

Prepare the given data set for visualization. Consider the following:¶

  • Are there any columns you can remove?
  • Are filters or groupings needed?
  • Are the data values structured for your chart types?

Clean the given data set for visualization using Python. Consider the following:¶

  • Are there any missing or invalid values?
  • Are there any unclear column names?
  • Are the data types correct for each column (e.g., numeric, categorical, datetime)?

Create multiple types of visualizations using Python. Include the following:¶

  • Dendrogram
  • PCA scatterplot
  • Cluster size distribution
  • Feature importance heatmap
  • Trend chart
  • Scatterplot
Note: You will need to ensure that you have created at least one of each of the visual types listed above.

Part 2: Reflection¶

This part is to be completed in a word document, using the output here to answer the topics.

Identify patterns in the data. Consider the following:¶

  • Are there any clear trends, clusters, or outliers visible in your visualizations?
  • Are certain variables showing consistent behavior or relationships?
  • Are the patterns similar across different visualization types?

Draw conclusions from the patterns. Consider the following:¶

  • Are your conclusions clearly based on the patterns you observed?
  • Are your findings supported by multiple visuals or data points?

Explain how the visualizations validate your findings. Consider the following:¶

  • Are specific chart elements (e.g., color, scale, labels) helping to highlight your findings?
  • Are the insights you found something you could not easily see without the visuals?

Write a summary of the visualization choices you made. Include the following:¶

  • An explanation of the types of charts you used
  • An explanation of the formatting decisions to support visual clarity

Import the Required Packages¶

  • pandas (pd): For reading and manipulating the dataset.
  • MinMaxScaler: A preprocessing tool from sklearn to normalize data values between 0 and 1.
  • PCA: Principal Component Analysis (dimensionality reduction) from sklearn for visualizing clusters in 2D.
  • dendrogram, linkage, fcluster: Tools from scipy for performing hierarchical clustering and visualizing its results.
  • matplotlib.pyplot (plt): For creating charts and saving visuals.
  • seaborn (sns): For advanced and visually appealing charts.
  • numpy (np): For numerical operations like arrays and aggregations.
In [1]:
import pandas as pd   # for reading & manipulating the dataset
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler    # a preprocessing tool from sklearn to normalize data values
                                                                                    # between 0 and 1
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA  # Principal Component Analysis (dimensionality reduction) from 
                                                                   # sklearn for visualizing clusters in 2D
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage, fcluster    # tools from scipy for performing hierarchical clustering & visualizing its results
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt     #  for creating charts & saving visuals
import seaborn as sns    #  for advanced & visually appealing charts
import numpy as np      # for numerical operations like arrays & aggregations

from IPython.display import Image, display # for image rendering in html output

import os  # NEW: create/check output folder for saved PNGs
import warnings  # NEW: optional, helps reduce noisy warnings in output
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # NEW: optional, keeps notebook output clean (can remove if you prefer seeing warnings)

# NEW: ensure output folder exists for saving charts
os.makedirs("output", exist_ok=True)  # ensures saved PNGs go to /output without errors

Part One: Data Visualization¶

Loading the Data¶

Hints: Use pd.read_csv to read a CSV file and load it into a DataFrame (data). Use try block to ensures the program handles errors gracefully if the file cannot be loaded (e.g., missing or incorrect path). Use exit() to stop the program if an error occurs.

print("Loading dataset...")

# To Do: Use the given dataset named "Most-Recent-Cohorts-Field-of-Study.csv" for this assignment
# Load this dataset
# For secure coding, put this action in a try/catch block

# NEW: Safety import in case the kernel restarted and the imports cell didn't run yet
# This prevents NameError if this cell is run independently
import pandas as pd

# NEW: Use glob to locate the file in the Codio workspace (e.g., inside /data)
# Codio sometimes places datasets in subfolders
import glob
import os

# NEW: Ensure output folder exists for saving charts later in the notebook
os.makedirs("output", exist_ok=True)

try:
    # NEW: Search recursively for the dataset file
    matches = glob.glob("**/Most-Recent-Cohorts-Field-of-Study.csv", recursive=True)
    if not matches:
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            "Dataset file not found anywhere. Make sure it exists in the Module Five Activity data folder."
        )

    # NEW: Use the first matching path found
    csv_path = matches[0]
    print("Found dataset at:", csv_path)

    # Load dataset into a pandas DataFrame
    data = pd.read_csv(csv_path, low_memory=False)

    print("Dataset loaded successfully.")
    print("Dataset shape:", data.shape)
    display(data.head())

except FileNotFoundError as e:
    # Explicit error for missing dataset
    print("Error:", e)
    raise

except Exception as e:
    # Catch-all for unexpected issues
    print("An unexpected error occurred while loading the dataset:")
    print(e)
    raise

Inspect and Select Numeric Columns¶

Hints: Use select_dtypes() to filter columns with numeric data types (float64 and int64). Removes columns like UNITID and OPEID6, which are not useful for clustering. Use dropna() to remove rows with missing values to clean data for clustering, see also module three sample for additional cleaning examples. Use error handling try blocks to ensures the program stops if the column selection fails.
In [6]:
print("Inspecting dataset to select numeric columns for clustering...")
# To Do: In a try/catch block, exclude identifiers 'UNITID' and 'OPEID6', 
#        then print the numeric columns selected for clustering and also print the data for clustering in rows & columns

try:
    # Select numeric columns only (int64 and float64)
    numeric_data = data.select_dtypes(include=["int64", "float64"])

    # Drop identifier columns if they exist (not useful for clustering)
    columns_to_drop = ["UNITID", "OPEID6"]
    numeric_data = numeric_data.drop(
        columns=[col for col in columns_to_drop if col in numeric_data.columns]
    )

    # NEW: Handle IPEDS privacy-suppressed values (e.g., "PS") by coercing to NaN
    # This ensures all remaining values are truly numeric
    numeric_data = numeric_data.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")

    # Remove rows with missing or invalid values to prepare clean clustering data
    numeric_data = numeric_data.dropna()

    # Display results
    print("Numeric columns selected for clustering:")
    print(numeric_data.columns.tolist())

    print("\nShape of clustering dataset (rows, columns):")
    print(numeric_data.shape)

    display(numeric_data.head())

except Exception as e:
    print("Error occurred while selecting numeric columns for clustering:")
    print(e)
    exit()

Normalize the Data¶

Hints: Use MinMaxScaler() to scale data values between 0 and 1, ensuring all features are on the same scale. Use fit_transform() to fit the scaler to the data and transform it.
In [7]:
print("Normalizing the data using MinMaxScaler...")
# To Do: in a try/catch block, normalize the data using MinMaxScaler

try:
    # NEW: Defensive check to ensure there is data to normalize
    if numeric_data.empty:
        raise ValueError("numeric_data is empty. Cannot perform normalization.")

    # Initialize the MinMaxScaler
    # MinMaxScaler scales all features to the range [0, 1],
    # which is important for distance-based methods like clustering and PCA
    scaler = MinMaxScaler()

    # Fit the scaler to the numeric data and transform it
    normalized_data = scaler.fit_transform(numeric_data)

    # Convert the normalized array back into a DataFrame
    normalized_df = pd.DataFrame(
        normalized_data,
        columns=numeric_data.columns,
        index=numeric_data.index
    )

    print("Data normalization completed successfully.")
    print("Shape of normalized dataset:", normalized_df.shape)
    display(normalized_df.head())

except Exception as e:
    print("Error occurred during data normalization:")
    print(e)
    exit()

Perform Hierarchical Clustering¶

Hints: Use linkage() to compute hierarchical clusters using Ward's method, which minimizes variance between clusters. Limit clustering to the first 1000 rows for performance. Use fcluster() to assign cluster labels to data points based on the number of clusters (max_clusters).
In [8]:
print("Performing hierarchical clustering using Ward's method...")
# To Do: in a try/catch block use the Ward's method to perform hierarchical clustering, limit max clusters to 4.

try:
    max_clusters = 4

    # Limit rows for performance (as instructed)
    clustering_input = normalized_df.iloc[:1000, :]

    # NEW: Defensive check (Ward linkage needs at least 2 rows)
    if clustering_input.shape[0] < 2:
        raise ValueError("Not enough rows to perform hierarchical clustering (need at least 2).")

    # NEW: Convert to NumPy array for SciPy (often more stable/faster than passing a DataFrame)
    clustering_array = clustering_input.to_numpy()

    # Compute linkage matrix using Ward's method
    Z = linkage(clustering_array, method="ward")

    # Assign cluster labels (1..max_clusters)
    cluster_labels = fcluster(Z, t=max_clusters, criterion="maxclust")

    print("Hierarchical clustering completed successfully.")
    print("Rows clustered:", clustering_input.shape[0])
    print("Number of clusters requested:", max_clusters)
    print("Cluster label counts:", pd.Series(cluster_labels).value_counts().sort_index().to_dict())

except Exception as e:
    print("Error occurred during hierarchical clustering:")
    print(e)
    exit()

Dendrogram¶

print("Creating dendrogram to visualize hierarchical clustering...")
# To Do: Create a dendrogram to visualize hierarchical clustering, and save the dendrogram into a png file under the 'output' folder.

try:
    import os

    # Ensure output folder exists
    os.makedirs("output", exist_ok=True)

    # NEW: Defensive check to ensure linkage matrix exists
    if "Z" not in globals():
        raise NameError("Linkage matrix Z not found. Run the clustering step before this cell.")

    # Create the dendrogram figure
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))

    # NEW: truncate_mode improves readability for large datasets
    dendrogram(
        Z,
        no_labels=True,
        truncate_mode="lastp",
        p=30,  # show only the last 30 merged clusters for clarity
        color_threshold=None
    )

    # Add clear labeling for readability
    plt.title("Hierarchical Clustering Dendrogram (Ward's Method)")
    plt.xlabel("Cluster Merge Index (Truncated)")
    plt.ylabel("Distance")

    # Save and close figure
    dendrogram_path = "output/dendrogram.png"
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(dendrogram_path, dpi=300)
    plt.close()

    print(f"Dendrogram saved to: {dendrogram_path}")

except Exception as e:
    print("Error occurred while creating/saving the dendrogram:")
    print(e)
    exit()

PCA Scatter Plot¶

Hints: A PCA scatter plot projects high-dimensional data into 2D using PCA for visualization. Save the image as pca_scatter_plot.png. Use display() to render the image for html file output. Do not use an html image tag in the markdown, or the image will not print in the html download.
In [11]:
print("Creating scatter plot (PCA Reduced) to visualize clusters in 2D...")
# To Do: Create a PCA Scatter Plot to visualize clusters in 2D, and save the PCA Scatter Plot into a png file under the 'output' folder.

try:
    import os

    # Ensure output folder exists
    os.makedirs("output", exist_ok=True)

    # NEW: Defensive checks
    if "normalized_df" not in globals() or "cluster_labels" not in globals():
        raise NameError("Required data not found. Ensure normalization and clustering steps ran successfully.")

    # Use the same rows used for clustering
    pca_input = normalized_df.iloc[:len(cluster_labels), :]

    # NEW: Convert to NumPy array for PCA stability
    pca_array = pca_input.to_numpy()

    # Run PCA to reduce to 2 components
    pca = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=42)
    pca_components = pca.fit_transform(pca_array)

    # Build a DataFrame for plotting
    pca_df = pd.DataFrame(
        pca_components,
        columns=["PC1", "PC2"],
        index=pca_input.index
    )
    pca_df["Cluster"] = cluster_labels

    # Create scatter plot
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    sns.scatterplot(
        data=pca_df,
        x="PC1",
        y="PC2",
        hue="Cluster",
        palette="tab10",
        alpha=0.8
    )

    # NEW: Include explained variance in the title (helps interpretation)
    explained_var = pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum() * 100
    plt.title(f"PCA Scatter Plot (2D) — {explained_var:.2f}% Variance Explained")
    plt.xlabel("Principal Component 1")
    plt.ylabel("Principal Component 2")
    plt.legend(title="Cluster", loc="best")

    # Save and close figure
    pca_path = "output/pca_scatter_plot.png"
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(pca_path, dpi=300)
    plt.close()

    print(f"PCA scatter plot saved to: {pca_path}")
    print("Explained variance ratio:", pca.explained_variance_ratio_)

except Exception as e:
    print("Error occurred while creating/saving the PCA scatter plot:")
    print(e)
    exit()

Trend Chart¶

Hints: A trend chart plots trends in a numeric feature across clusters. Save the image as trend_chart.png. Use display() to render the image for html file output. Do not use an html image tag in the markdown, or the image will not print in the html download.
In [17]:
print("Creating trend chart to analyze a numeric feature across clusters...")
# To Do: Create a trend chart to analyze a numeric feature across clusters, and save it into a png file under the 'output' folder.

try:
    import os

    # Ensure output folder exists
    os.makedirs("output", exist_ok=True)

    # Align raw data to the same rows used for clustering
    trend_raw = data.iloc[:len(cluster_labels), :].copy()
    trend_raw["Cluster"] = cluster_labels

    # Try to find a "time" column (common names)
    candidate_time_cols = ["YEAR", "Year", "year", "CohortYear", "cohort_year", "TERM_YEAR", "term_year"]
    time_col = next((c for c in candidate_time_cols if c in trend_raw.columns), None)

    # Identify numeric columns (exclude ID-like columns if present)
    numeric_cols = trend_raw.select_dtypes(include=["int64", "float64"]).columns.tolist()
    for drop_col in ["UNITID", "OPEID6"]:
        if drop_col in numeric_cols:
            numeric_cols.remove(drop_col)

    if len(numeric_cols) == 0:
        raise ValueError("No numeric columns available to build a trend chart.")

    # NEW: Avoid low-information columns/codes for the trend feature
    # (Old) bad_cols = {"MAIN", "CIPCODE", "CREDLEV"}  # common “not helpful” numeric columns for trending
    # NEW: Expand bad_cols to reduce the chance we pick an identifier/coded column by accident
    bad_cols = {"MAIN", "CIPCODE", "CREDLEV", "CONTROL", "UNITID", "OPEID6", "IPEDSCOUNT1"}

    filtered_cols = [c for c in numeric_cols if c not in bad_cols]

    # NEW: If filtering removes everything, fall back to numeric_cols
    if len(filtered_cols) == 0:
        filtered_cols = numeric_cols

    # NEW: Pick the numeric feature with the most variance (more informative than "first column")
    tmp = trend_raw[filtered_cols].dropna()

    # NEW: Print top variance candidates (helps justify feature selection / reflection)
    if not tmp.empty:
        top_var = tmp.var().sort_values(ascending=False).head(5)
        print("Top variance numeric candidates:", top_var.to_dict())

    feature_col = tmp.var().sort_values(ascending=False).index[0] if not tmp.empty else filtered_cols[0]

    if time_col is not None:
        # Ensure time column is numeric for sorting/grouping
        trend_raw[time_col] = pd.to_numeric(trend_raw[time_col], errors="coerce")

        # Drop rows where time or feature is missing
        plot_df = trend_raw.dropna(subset=[time_col, feature_col])

        # Compute mean feature over time per cluster
        grouped = (
            plot_df.groupby([time_col, "Cluster"])[feature_col]
            .mean()
            .reset_index()
            .sort_values(time_col)
        )

        # Plot lines: one per cluster
        plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
        sns.lineplot(
            data=grouped,
            x=time_col,
            y=feature_col,
            hue="Cluster",
            marker="o"
        )

        plt.title(f"Trend Chart: Mean {feature_col} Over {time_col} by Cluster")
        plt.xlabel(time_col)
        plt.ylabel(f"Mean {feature_col}")

    else:
        # Fallback: trend "across clusters" using mean feature per cluster
        grouped = (
            trend_raw.dropna(subset=[feature_col])
            .groupby("Cluster")[feature_col]
            .mean()
            .reset_index()
            .sort_values("Cluster")
        )

        plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
        sns.lineplot(
            data=grouped,
            x="Cluster",
            y=feature_col,
            marker="o"
        )

        # NEW: Make it extra explicit this is a cluster-based trend (since no time column exists)
        plt.title(f"Trend Chart: Mean {feature_col} by Cluster (No Time Column Found)")
        plt.xlabel("Cluster")
        plt.ylabel(f"Mean {feature_col}")

    # Save and close figure
    trend_path = "output/trend_chart.png"
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(trend_path, dpi=300)
    plt.close()

    print(f"Trend chart saved to: {trend_path}")
    print("Time column used:" , time_col if time_col else "None (fallback used)")
    print("Feature trended:", feature_col)

except Exception as e:
    print("Error occurred while creating/saving the trend chart:")
    print(e)
    exit()

Scatter Plot¶

Hints: A scatter plot explores the relationship between two features, grouped by clusters. Save the image as scatter_plot.png. Use display() to render the image for html file output. Do not use an html image tag in the markdown, or the image will not print in the html download.
In [19]:
print("Creating scatter plot of two features...")
# To Do: Create a scatter plot of two features, and save it into a png file under the 'output' folder.

try:
    import os

    # Ensure output folder exists
    os.makedirs("output", exist_ok=True)

    # Align raw data to the same rows used for clustering
    scatter_df = data.iloc[:len(cluster_labels), :].copy()
    scatter_df["Cluster"] = cluster_labels

    # Select numeric columns (exclude ID-like columns if present)
    numeric_cols = scatter_df.select_dtypes(include=["int64", "float64"]).columns.tolist()
    for drop_col in ["UNITID", "OPEID6"]:
        if drop_col in numeric_cols:
            numeric_cols.remove(drop_col)

    if len(numeric_cols) < 2:
        raise ValueError("Need at least two numeric columns to create a scatter plot.")

    # Avoid low-information or code-like numeric columns
    bad_cols = {"MAIN", "CIPCODE", "CREDLEV"}
    filtered_cols = [c for c in numeric_cols if c not in bad_cols]

    # Fallback if filtering removes too many columns
    if len(filtered_cols) < 2:
        filtered_cols = numeric_cols

    # Select two features with the highest variance (most informative)
    tmp = scatter_df[filtered_cols].dropna()
    if tmp.shape[1] < 2 or tmp.empty:
        x_col, y_col = filtered_cols[0], filtered_cols[1]
    else:
        top_cols = tmp.var().sort_values(ascending=False).index.tolist()
        x_col, y_col = top_cols[0], top_cols[1]

    # Remove rows missing either feature
    plot_df = scatter_df.dropna(subset=[x_col, y_col])

    # Create scatter plot
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    sns.scatterplot(
        data=plot_df,
        x=x_col,
        y=y_col,
        hue="Cluster",
        palette="tab10",
        alpha=0.75
    )

    plt.title(f"Scatter Plot: {x_col} vs {y_col} (Colored by Cluster)")
    plt.xlabel(x_col)
    plt.ylabel(y_col)
    plt.legend(title="Cluster")

    # Save and close figure
    scatter_path = "output/scatter_plot.png"
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(scatter_path, dpi=300)
    plt.close()

    print(f"Scatter plot saved to: {scatter_path}")
    print("X feature:", x_col)
    print("Y feature:", y_col)

except Exception as e:
    print("Error occurred while creating/saving the scatter plot:")
    print(e)
    exit()
